summary: Sarah dies at Hebron, and Abraham patiently buys the double cave for her burial despite the earlier promise of the land. The chapter then names Rebecca, Keturah's six sons, and the twins Jacob and Esau before Abraham blesses Jacob in Rebecca’s presence.
whyItMatters: The land promise meets the practical cost of a burial place, and the family story shifts from Abraham to a contested choice between Isaac's sons.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: Hebron and Abraham's family in the years after the mountain test, extending to Jacob and Esau's youth.
context.literaryForm: Burial account and genealogy followed by ancestral blessing poetry.

before.text: Isaac has been spared on the mountain and Abraham has returned safely to Beersheba.

here.text: Sarah’s burial and the births of a new generation lead to Abraham’s blessing of Jacob.

after.text: Abraham next summons all his sons and grandsons for a broad final instruction, then gives Isaac specific ritual commands.

outline.heading: Sarah’s death and purchased burial place
outline.note: Abraham buys the cave and the narrator names this a trial.

outline.heading: Rebecca, Keturah, and the twins
outline.note: Marriages and births move the family line forward.

outline.heading: Abraham speaks to Rebecca about Jacob
outline.note: He states his preference and the blessings he expects for Jacob.

outline.heading: Abraham blesses Jacob
outline.note: The blessing is given before Rebecca as parental preferences are restated.

keyVerses.text: And they besought him saying, We shall give it to thee for nothing; but he would not take it from their hands for nothing, for he gave the price of the place, the money in full, and he bowed down before them twice, and after this he buried his dead in the double cave.
keyVerses.why: Abraham pays the full price for Sarah's burial place despite being offered it without payment.

keyVerses.text: 'Jacob, my beloved son, whom my soul loveth, may God bless thee from above the firmament, and may He give thee all the blessings wherewith He blessed Adam, and Enoch, and Noah, and Shem; and all the things of which He told me, and all the things which He promised to give me, may he cause to cleave to thee and to thy seed for ever, according to the days of heaven above the earth.
keyVerses.why: The blessing transfers the ancestral promises to Jacob before the later inheritance conflicts.

questions.question: Why does Abraham buy a grave if the land was promised to him?
questions.answer: The narrator calls his patient negotiation another test and says he did not invoke the promise as a demand. He pays the full price for Sarah’s burial site, distinguishing future promise from immediate possession.

questions.question: What is the “double cave”?
questions.answer: It is the burial place near Hebron that Abraham obtains from the children of Heth. The chapter describes its purchase and Sarah’s burial there, rather than treating it as a palace or worship shrine.

questions.question: Does the paid purchase mean the surrounding people had no rights in the land?
questions.answer: The story shows Abraham asking the children of Heth for a place and paying their stated price. Whatever one makes of the larger land promise, the scene itself does not portray Abraham simply taking the burial property by force.

questions.question: Who enters the family story after Sarah’s death?
questions.answer: Rebecca becomes Isaac’s wife, Abraham has six sons with Keturah, and Rebecca later bears Jacob and Esau. These names prepare the next part of the ancestral narrative.

questions.question: Why is Esau judged so sharply here?
questions.answer: The narrator contrasts Jacob’s writing and uprightness with Esau’s hunting, war, and fierceness, then reports Abraham’s preference. Those are this work’s character judgments; readers should not treat a person’s work in the field as itself a moral failing.

questions.question: What does Abraham ask for Jacob in his blessing?
questions.answer: He asks God to pass on promises associated with earlier ancestors, protect Jacob’s line from Mastêmâ’s spirits, and keep a fatherly relationship with the people. The blessing is a prayer and claim within the story, not an account of events already completed.

questions.question: How do family affections differ at the end?
questions.answer: Rebecca and Abraham favor Jacob, while Isaac loves Esau more. The chapter makes that division plain before the brothers’ later conflicts over birthright and marriage.

glossary.def: The people from whom Abraham requests and buys Sarah’s burial place.
A spoken wish or invocation for God’s favor and a descendant’s future.
